Yes. 

The story is a cohesive and deeply unified whole where the external plot and internal character arc seamlessly interweave. 

In the beginning, Martin is established as a solitary, defensive man who values the appearance of competence (carrying a second walking stick he doesn't need) and insists on being technically right at the expense of emotional connection (the argument over the saucepan, and his defensive phone call with his son, Daniel). 

In the middle, his discovery of the car crash forces him into a situation where his competence fails—he cannot save the woman. As he waits with her body, the silence prompts him to examine his past: his career inspecting what lies "underneath" bridges, his overprotective impulse with his young son, and his rigid refusal to comfort his dying mother until his ex-wife intervened. Even his realization that he is unfairly using the dead woman as a confessor shows self-awareness and growth.

This logically and emotionally leads to the end. Having confronted mortality and his own stubborn isolation, Martin accepts help (wearing the rescuer's oversized jacket) and reaches out to his son. When he tells Daniel, "I'm here," it serves as a thematic resolution—he is no longer waiting for his son "to become a different person," but is instead making himself emotionally present. Every memory and detail in the story serves to propel Martin toward this quiet, satisfying transformation.
